title: Finishing Drywall
short_answer: Three coats, each wider and thinner, only on dry mud — scrape between. Finish to the specified GA-214 level, not nicer than priced.
summary: Finishing is where the labor is, where the reputation is, and where the two get traded against each other by accident.
plain_words: Three coats, each one wider and thinner than the last, each one only over a coat that's fully dry. Scrape between them. Then sand — and if you did the coats right, sanding is just blending the edges, not reshaping the wall. The biggest mistake isn't doing it badly; it's doing it better than the job was priced for.
when_to_use: Scrapping Status done and room accepted for tape

Any coat-sequence question on a drywall finish
prerequisites: Conditions: temperature and air movement for mud

materials.name: All-purpose / topping / setting compound as specified
Paper or mesh tape per detail

steps.body: Room is scraped and accepted. Don't start tape in a room that isn't ready — you'll do the scrapper's work at a taper's rate.
Pre-fill oversized gaps with setting compound and let them set before taping over.
Conditions reasonable — mud needs temperature and air movement. Cold, damp, still air turns a three-day finish into a week.
Full bed of compound behind the tape — tape bedded in a starved joint blisters and comes back.
Squeeze the tape down firmly and clean out the excess. Every bit you leave now is something somebody sands later.
Corner bead set straight and secure — a wavy bead can't be fixed with mud, only hidden badly.
Only over a fully dry previous coat. Coating over damp compound causes shrinkage cracks and delamination that show up after paint.
Wider than the first. Every coat gets wider — that's how a joint disappears.
Butt joints get the widest treatment on the wall. Scrape the ridges before they harden.
Thin, wide, feathered. This coat blends, it doesn't fill.
Lightweight or topping compound — sands far easier, on the coat that gets sanded most.
Sanding blends edges. Don't over-sand — cutting into the paper creates fuzz that telegraphs through paint.
Check with a bright light at a low angle. That's the light a paint job will reveal.
Vacuum-assisted sanding where dust control matters — occupied buildings, phased work, other trades nearby.
Match specified texture and any existing texture on a tie-in. Make a sample and get it approved.

warnings.title: Finishing above the price
warnings.body: The biggest mistake isn’t doing it badly — it’s finishing better than the job was priced for. Match the specified level.

warnings.title: Coating green mud
warnings.body: Only coat over a fully dry previous coat. Green mud shrinks, cracks, and delaminates later.

warnings.title: Tape without scrape
warnings.body: Don’t start tape in a room that isn’t scraped — you’ll do scrapper work at taper rates.

common_mistakes.title: Starved tape bed
common_mistakes.right: Full bed behind tape, squeeze excess

common_mistakes.title: Sanding to reshape
common_mistakes.wrong: Heavy sand to fix thick ridges
common_mistakes.right: Scrape between coats; sand only blends edges
common_mistakes.why: Sanding into paper ruins the face

troubleshooting.likely_cause: Coat not wide enough or sanded too early
troubleshooting.fix: Raking light; re-coat wider on dry mud; check level vs sheen
